text: Calling one operation from Python, as in the last lesson, is the smallest possible example. The real workflow — initializing a target profile, running many shots efficiently, inspecting resource estimates, and submitting to Azure Quantum — is what you'll actually use on a real project.

Four pieces make up that real workflow: qsharp.init sets up the target profile, determining which Q# features and gate sets you're compiling against. qsharp.run does repeated sampling natively, in one call, faster and more idiomatic than a Python loop. qsharp.estimate pulls a resource-estimate report into the same Python session. And the azure-quantum package's Workspace hands a compiled program off to the cloud, the same submission model from Chapter 3, invoked from right here.

qsharp.init with a target profile sets up the compilation target before you run anything. A profile matching real hardware is more restrictive than the default simulator-oriented profile, since fault-tolerant-era hardware won't support arbitrary mid-circuit classical logic the way a simulator can. Code that compiles fine against the permissive default can fail against a restrictive hardware profile — catching that locally, before submission, is exactly what initializing against the right profile up front is for.

Last lesson's Counter over a Python loop works, but it calls back into the Q# runtime once per shot. qsharp.run does the equivalent sampling natively in one call — both faster and the version you'd actually call in real experiment code, once you're past a one-off sanity check.

The resource estimator from Chapter 3 isn't CLI-only — the same qsharp package produces an estimate directly in a Python session, letting you fold feasibility checking into the same script as your correctness checks. And once you're ready to move beyond local simulation, azure-quantum's Workspace connects that same compiled program to a real workspace target — qsharp handles local compilation and simulation, azure-quantum handles the cloud submission, both operating on the same underlying program.

Next lesson scales this up from one notebook cell to a real repository: a project layout that keeps the quantum algorithm and the Python orchestration as clearly separate, independently testable concerns.
